guide.title: Unit 4: Short Fiction II: review guide
guide.intro: This unit looks more closely at how characters come into conflict, how they respond to the places they live in, and how the way a story is narrated (close inside a mind, or from a distance) shapes what readers notice.

sections.title: Conflict, relationships, and archetypes
body: The protagonist is the character whose desires drive the story; an antagonist is whatever opposes them, which may be another person, a group, nature, or part of the protagonist's own mind. Conflict can be external (between characters or with the world) or internal (within one character).

An archetype is a character type or pattern that recurs across many stories, such as the wise mentor, the journey, or the outsider. Recognizing an archetype helps you see what a reader expects, and then what the writer does with or against that expectation.
points: Name the conflict precisely: who or what opposes whom, and over what.
An archetype is a starting point for analysis, not a conclusion; ask how this character differs from the type.

sections.title: Characters and setting
body: Characters act on their setting and are shaped by it. A place can test a character, mirror a character's state of mind, or press on a character's choices.
When a setting detail seems to echo a mood (a dry fountain in a heat wave, a brown field in the rain), ask what it shows about the characters who move through it.
points: Explain how the setting functions, not only what it looks like.
Notice how a character treats a place; it can reveal what they value or fear.

sections.title: Narration, distance, and tone
body: Stream of consciousness narration follows a character's thoughts as they flow, often in long, loosely linked sentences that jump between present sensations and memories.

Narrative distance is how close the narration stays to a character's mind. A narrator looking back years later may understand what a young character could not. Tone is the narrator's attitude toward the subject, shown through word choice and detail.
points: Ask what the narrator knows, and when the narrator learned it.
Describe tone with precise words (restrained, wry, tender), not just “positive” or “negative.”

example.prompt: A story's narrator says: “I was eight that winter, and I thought the snow had come for me.” What does this sentence reveal about narrative distance?
example.solution: The narrator is an adult looking back (“I was eight”), so the story can show both the child's view (the snow came for me) and the adult's quiet recognition that the belief was a child's. A claim might be: “The adult narrator treats the child's wonder with tenderness rather than correction.”

misconceptions: An antagonist is any opposing force, including nature, society, or the protagonist's own fear.
“Stream of consciousness is just careless writing.”
Its run-on style is deliberate: it imitates how thoughts move.
“Calling a character an archetype is enough analysis.”
Explain what the archetype does in this story and how the writer uses or changes it.
“A first-person narrator always knows everything about the story.”
A narrator may understand only part of what happened, or understand it only later.

passages.title: Passage 1: from a story about two brothers and a farm
text: (1) Ray had stayed. That was the whole of the argument, as far as he was concerned, and he made it again at the kitchen table while his brother Owen turned his hat in his hands. “Twenty years I've run this place. You sent a card at Christmas.”

(2) Owen did not answer at once. He looked past Ray to the window, where the north field lay brown under a thin rain, and he thought of the letter from the bank folded in his coat pocket, the one Ray had not opened.
(3) “I'm not here to take it from you,” Owen said at last. “I'm here because it's already being taken.”
(4) Ray laughed, a short sound with no pleasure in it, and stood to put the kettle on, which was what their father had always done when he wanted a conversation to end.

passages.title: Passage 2: from a story about a bus stop
text: (1) The 42 was late again, of course it was late, it was always late on Thursdays, and Teresa counted the cracks in the shelter's plastic wall, seven, eight, the one shaped like a river, the river behind her mother's house where they had thrown bread to the ducks, did ducks still come there, did anyone, her mother would have said stop fretting, Teresa, the bus comes when it comes.
(2) A man beside her was eating an orange. The smell was so sharp and so sudden that for a moment she was nine years old and holding a peeled orange in both hands like a lamp.
(3) Then the bus came, wheezing, and she climbed on and showed her pass and sat by the window, and she did not look back at the shelter, or at the man, or at the crack shaped like a river.

passages.title: Passage 3: from a story about a heat wave
text: (1) In the fourth week of the heat, the city stopped pretending. Shops kept their grates half down at noon; the fountain in Delancey Square was switched off and filled with dry leaves; and old Mr. Sato, who had swept his front step every morning for thirty years, left the broom leaning against the door.

(2) Only Benny, who was eleven and had nowhere else to be, still went out. He walked the length of the avenue in the white glare, touching each lamppost as he passed it, as though the street might come apart if someone did not keep count.

(3) I was sixteen that summer, and I watched him from the window. I can say now, so many years later, what neither of us could have said then: that our father had left in June, and that the counting was a kind of prayer.

passages.title: Passage 4: from a story about a ferry
text: (1) The ferryman was older than anyone in the village could remember, and he had a way of looking at a passenger as if he already knew where they were going, and why.

(2) Ana was fourteen when she asked to learn the river. He gave her the pole without a word and let her push them out into the current, and when the boat swung sideways and she nearly lost it, he said only, “The river is not your enemy. Your hurry is.”

(3) She came every morning that spring. By June she could read the water, the slick that meant a sunken log, the ripple over a sandbar, and the morning he did not come down to the landing, she took the boat across alone, as if she had always known she would.

questions.prompt: The central conflict in the passage is primarily between
choices: Ray and his late father over how to run the farm
Owen and the weather, which has ruined the north field and with it the year's harvest
Owen and the bank officer who wrote the letter
Ray and Owen, over the farm and who has the right to speak about its future
questions.explanation: The brothers argue at the kitchen table: Ray claims the farm because he stayed, and Owen brings news Ray does not want to hear.
choiceExplanations: The father is mentioned only in the final comparison; he takes no part in the argument.
The rain is part of the setting, not the source of the conflict.
The bank never appears; the letter is a source of the brothers' tension.

questions.prompt: The narration in paragraph 2, which reports Owen's thoughts, allows the reader to know
choices: that Ray secretly plans to sell the farm
about the bank letter, which Ray has not read
that Owen wants to move back to the farm
what Ray thinks of his brother's Christmas cards
questions.explanation: The narrator enters Owen's mind and reveals the folded bank letter “the one Ray had not opened,” so the reader knows more than Ray does.
choiceExplanations: Nothing suggests Ray plans to sell; he insists on keeping it.
Owen says he is not there to take the farm.
The narration reports Owen's thoughts, not Ray's.

questions.prompt: The description of the north field that “lay brown under a thin rain” (paragraph 2) mainly serves to
choices: explain why Owen arrived late
show that the farm, after a long dry spell, is about to have a good harvest
establish that the story takes place in summer
mirror the farm's decline and the gloom of the meeting
questions.explanation: Owen looks at the field as he thinks of the bank letter; the dull, wet field echoes the farm's trouble and the mood in the kitchen.
choiceExplanations: The passage says nothing about Owen arriving late.
A brown field in thin rain suggests failure, not plenty.
The image suggests a bleak season; nothing points to summer.

questions.prompt: Ray's decision to put the kettle on in paragraph 4 most strongly suggests that he
choices: is offering Owen hospitality, a sign that he has calmly accepted his brother's news
has decided to open the bank letter after all
wants to show that he is calmer than his brother
is ending the talk as his father used to, avoiding a truth he won't face
questions.explanation: The narrator says this was what their father did “when he wanted a conversation to end,” so Ray repeats a family habit of shutting down conflict instead of facing the news.
choiceExplanations: His laugh has “no pleasure in it,” and the father comparison signals refusal, not acceptance.
Nothing suggests he has opened the letter.
The gesture is linked to ending conversations, not to calm.

questions.prompt: The long, loosely linked sentence in paragraph 1 is best described as
choices: stream of consciousness that follows Teresa's thoughts as they wander
objective reporting of events in the order they occurred, as a detached observer would see them
a dialogue between Teresa and her mother
a formal description of the bus schedule
questions.explanation: The sentence moves from the late bus to cracks in the wall to a river and her mother's voice, the way thoughts drift: stream of consciousness.
choiceExplanations: The narration follows Teresa's mind, not an outside view of events.
Her mother's words are only imagined (“would have said”); no conversation takes place.
The schedule is mentioned only as a complaint, not described formally.

questions.prompt: The crack in the shelter wall “shaped like a river” (paragraph 1) functions mainly to
choices: carry Teresa's thoughts from the shelter to memories of home
foreshadow a flood later in the story
show that the bus shelter is unsafe
suggest that the city's rivers are polluted and that the damage has reached even the bus shelters
questions.explanation: The crack reminds her of the river behind her mother's house, so an ordinary detail of the setting opens a path into memory.
choiceExplanations: No flood is suggested; the river belongs to her past.
Nothing suggests danger; the crack prompts a memory.
The passage says nothing about pollution.

questions.prompt: The effect of the orange's smell on Teresa (paragraph 2) suggests that she
choices: dislikes the man and wants to move away
is afraid of the strangers around her
is easily carried back into her childhood by small sensations
is hungry after a long day and wishes the man would share his orange
questions.explanation: A sudden smell makes her “nine years old” again for a moment: her present keeps opening onto her past.
choiceExplanations: She shows no dislike of the man.
Nothing suggests fear.
The passage describes memory, not hunger.

questions.prompt: Compared with paragraph 1, the narration in paragraph 3 is
choices: more orderly and focused on actions, as Teresa turns away from her memories
focused on the thoughts of the man eating the orange
even more crowded with memories than paragraph 1
shifted into the first person, so that Teresa speaks directly to the reader about her memories
questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 lists actions in order (climbed on, showed her pass, sat) and says she “did not look back” at the crack: the drifting thoughts stop as she closes off the past.
choiceExplanations: The man is mentioned only as something she does not look back at.
Paragraph 3 contains no memories at all.
The narration stays in the third person (“she”).

questions.prompt: Details in paragraph 1 such as the half-lowered grates and the dry fountain mainly convey
choices: the first cool days of autumn
a neighborhood under construction for the summer
a city preparing for a holiday
a city worn down and slowed by the heat
questions.explanation: Shops half close, the fountain is shut off, and even Mr. Sato stops sweeping: the heat has made the city give up its routines.
choiceExplanations: It is the “fourth week of the heat,” not a cool season.
No construction is mentioned.
Nothing festive is described.

questions.prompt: Benny's habit of touching each lamppost (paragraph 2) most likely reflects his
choices: game with friends who are following him
need to hold on to some order in a world that feels unstable
confusion about which street he lives on, since the heat has made the avenue look strange
plan to repair the street lights
questions.explanation: The narrator says he touched them “as though the street might come apart if someone did not keep count,” a small ritual of control.
choiceExplanations: He walks alone; no friends are mentioned.
Nothing suggests he is lost.
The touching is a ritual, not a repair.

questions.prompt: Paragraph 3 reveals that the narrator is
choices: an outsider with no connection to Benny's family who happened to see him that summer
Mr. Sato, watching from across the street
Benny's older sibling, recalling the summer many years later
Benny himself as an adult
questions.explanation: The narrator was “sixteen that summer,” watched Benny from the window, and speaks of “our father,” so the narrator is an older sibling looking back.
choiceExplanations: “Our father” shows the narrator belongs to Benny's family.
Mr. Sato is described in the third person in paragraph 1.
The narrator watched “him,” so the narrator is not Benny.

questions.prompt: The distance between the adult narrator and the events (paragraph 3) affects the passage chiefly by
choices: making the events seem invented and unreliable
hiding the reason for Benny's behavior from the reader until the story's very last line
letting the narrator name a meaning the children could not have put into words
creating suspense about whether the father will leave
questions.explanation: Looking back “so many years later,” the narrator can name what the counting meant (a prayer after the father left), which the children could not have said then.
choiceExplanations: Nothing signals that the memory is false; distance adds understanding.
Paragraph 3 reveals the reason rather than hiding it.
The father has already left (“in June”); there is no suspense about it.

questions.prompt: The ferryman most closely fits which character archetype?
choices: The wise mentor who guides a younger person
The villain who blocks the young hero's path
The fool whose mistakes bring laughter
The trickster who deceives others
questions.explanation: He is ageless, seems to know where people are going, teaches Ana with few words, and then disappears: the pattern of the wise mentor.
choiceExplanations: He helps Ana rather than opposing her.
His words are wise, not foolish.
He never deceives anyone.

questions.prompt: In paragraph 1, the narrator describes the ferryman from a distance that
choices: reveals his private thoughts about each passenger
emphasizes how mysterious he seems to the village
mocks the villagers for their superstitions
lets him tell his own story in the first person
questions.explanation: The narrator reports what the village sees (older than anyone “could remember,” a look “as if he already knew”), never his inner thoughts, which keeps him mysterious.
choiceExplanations: His thoughts are never given; the narrator says only how he looks at passengers.
The tone is respectful, not mocking.
The passage is in the third person.

questions.prompt: The river in the passage functions mainly as
choices: a danger that ends Ana's life
a challenge through which Ana's growing skill and patience are measured
a symbol of the village's wealth
a background with no real effect on the characters or on what they learn
questions.explanation: Ana nearly loses the boat at first; by June she can “read the water” and crosses alone. The river is the test that shows her growth.
choiceExplanations: Ana succeeds; she is not harmed.
Nothing links the river to wealth.
The river shapes everything Ana learns.

questions.prompt: The final sentence of the passage most strongly suggests that
choices: Ana has taken the boat without permission
Ana regrets the time she spent learning the river
Ana has taken the ferryman's place, completing the pattern in which a mentor passes on his knowledge
the ferryman has moved to another village, where he will begin to teach someone else the river
questions.explanation: When he does not come, she crosses “as if she had always known she would”: the apprentice becomes the new ferryman, as the mentor pattern leads readers to expect.
choiceExplanations: “As if she had always known” presents the crossing as fitting, not as theft.
Nothing suggests regret.
The passage does not say where he has gone; the focus is on Ana taking up his role.
